newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan's import car sales growth slows slightly.
newsitem.headline: Japan's import car sales growth slows slightly.

text.p: The boom in imported car sales in Japan is likely to be a little less sonic in 1996, industry sources said on Friday.
After jumping almost 29 percent last year to a record 388,162 units, sales have grown only by about 12 percent so far this year, the Japan Automobile Importers Association said.
That would leave sales for the year short of a goal of 450,000 units set by the association, mainly due to a fall in sales of cars made overseas by Japanese companies.
Sales of imported vehicles hit a record 38,017 units in September, up 5.7 percent from the same month last year, the association announced on Friday.
That follows a drop in August to 26,542 units, the first year-on-year fall in 34 months.
"It will be tough to reach 450,000 units because Toyota decided to stop producing its Scepter station wagon in the United States," association planning manager Ken Kano told Reuters.
Last December, the importers' body forecast sales of imported vehicles of 450,000 units in 1996.
Sales for the January to September period totalled 319,983 units, up 12.4 percent from the same period a year earlier.
Sales needed to rise 15.9 percent for the year to reach 450,000, which Kano admitted would now be difficult. "It will be tough to gain 15 percent now for the whole year," he said.
Toyota Motors's Toyota Motor Manufacturing Kentucky in Georgetown, Kentucky, stopped making the Scepter in June because of poor demand in the United States.
"Sales of imported vehicles are likely to total about 438,000 in 1996, less than the projected 450,000, mainly because of the loss of the Scepter sales," Nomura Research analyst Seiji Sugiura said.
Sales of vehicles produced by the overseas units of Japanese makers fell 27.9 percent from a year earlier to 7,121 in September, mainly due to lower sales of the Scepter.
But sales of cars made by foreign makers climbed and will continue to do so, Kano said.

Volkswagen topped the list in September with sales of 5,757 units, up 97.6 percent from a year earlier, mainly helped by strong demand for the compact Polo and the Golf Wagon, a Volkswagen Group Japan KK spokeswoman said.
Mercedes-Benz was second with sales of 4,274 cars, up 16 percent, due to good demand for its E-class cars, a Mercedes-Benz Japan Co Ltd spokeswoman said.
Honda Motor sold 4,015 units, up 12.5 percent. The strong sales should carry over into October because of good demand for the partially remodelled U.S.-made Accord Wagons, a Honda spokesman said.
General Motors Corp sold 2,102 units, up 104 percent, in September, including 1,129 Cavaliers through Toyota's sales network with Toyota's nameplate.
Chrysler's sales rose 46.6 percent to 2,034 units in September.
Chrysler and Honda sales were up partly because Honda dealers sold off damaged Chrysler Cherokees and Honda Accord Wagons at cheap prices.
A freak hailstorm north of Tokyo on July 3 damaged 6,000 to 7,000 cars, including U.S.-made Chrysler Cherokees and Honda Accord Wagons.
